title: Acquire Infrastructure: Botnet
summary: Under Acquire Infrastructure, this sub-technique focuses on obtaining an existing network of compromised machines rather than building one. The operator buys or subscribes to a botnet, often through a booter or stresser service that rents out attack capacity, and then uses it for follow-on activity such as large-scale phishing, distributed denial of service, or traffic relaying. Internet-facing edge devices and unsupported end-of-life appliances are commonly bundled into these networks because they are rarely patched and seldom monitored, and operational relay box networks composed of virtual private servers, small office routers, and internet of things devices are leased for the same purpose. The capability is therefore rented as a service, so no exploitation appears in the buyer's own logs. Defenders rarely see the purchase; they see the consequence, which is a flood of requests or authentication attempts from many unrelated consumer addresses, each individually unremarkable, plus provider abuse reports and sudden traffic growth that no single source explains.

beginner.definition: A botnet is a group of computers that a criminal controls without the owners knowing. This sub-technique is about an attacker renting or buying such a group. The parent technique covers getting infrastructure in general. Here the thing obtained is other people's infected machines.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rented attack capacity lets one person behave like thousands. They can flood a website, send huge amounts of spam, or spread malware from many places at once. The infected machines belong to ordinary homes and offices, so the traffic looks normal and tracing it back is very hard.
howItWorks: An operator builds a botnet by infecting routers, cameras, and other devices that face the internet.
The operator then sells access to it, usually as a monthly subscription to an attack service.
A buyer pays, then sends a target address and a start time through a web panel.
A control server tells every infected device to send requests to that target at once.
The same rented machines may also carry phishing mail or hide the buyer's real servers.
Owners of the infected devices usually notice nothing, so the network stays available for reuse.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where the landlord has handed spare keys to strangers. Each flat looks normal from the street, and each tenant minds their own business. Together they can make a great deal of noise at a neighbour's door, and that neighbour cannot tell which tenant is responsible.
takeaways: Traffic from many unrelated consumer addresses at once is the usual sign of a rented botnet.
Old, unsupported network devices are the easiest machines for criminals to recruit.
Rate limits and filters reduce the harm even when you cannot identify the operator.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Acquire Infrastructure technique.
Describe how booter and stresser services turn a botnet into a purchasable capability.
Identify the traffic patterns and log sources that reveal botnet-sourced activity.
Distinguish coordinated attack traffic from ordinary spikes in legitimate demand.
Describe how filtering and capacity planning limit the impact of rented attack traffic.
